`pkgres` (semver ranges plus a backtracking dependency resolver) has several reported bugs.
Find and fix their causes; README.md documents the intended semantics. Keep all other
existing behaviour unchanged.

1. Prerelease numbers are compared as text. `Version.parse("1.0.0-alpha.2") <
   Version.parse("1.0.0-alpha.10")` is False (it should be True, per semver: numeric
   identifiers compare as numbers). Sorting, `max_satisfying(["1.0.0-beta.2",
   "1.0.0-beta.11"], ">=1.0.0-beta.1")` (returns beta.2, should be beta.11), `diff` upgrade /
   downgrade labels and the resolver's "highest version first" choice are all affected.

2. Caret ranges on 0.x versions are too narrow. `^0.2.3` is documented as `>=0.2.3 <0.3.0`
   but `parse_range("^0.2.3").matches("0.2.9")` is False. Likewise `^0.12.0`, `^0.10.1` and
   `^0.2.3-beta.1`. (`^0.0.3`, `^0.0`, `^0`, `^0.2` and `^1.2.3` follow the README rules.)

3. Ranges that name only a major number stay inside the first minor. `~1` matches `1.0.x`
   only (`1.5.0` is rejected, should be accepted), `1`, `1.x`, `1.*` and `=1` likewise. `<=1`
   rejects `1.5.0`, `>1` accepts `1.5.0`, `1.2.3 - 2` rejects `2.5.0`, and `^0` rejects
   `0.4.0`. Fix the cause, not only the one form.

4. The resolver fails on solvable inputs after backtracking. Index: `A` 1.0.0 needs
   `C ^1.0.0`, `A` 2.0.0 needs `C ^2.0.0`, `B` 1.0.0 needs `C ^1.0.0`, `C` has 1.0.0, 1.5.0,
   2.0.0. `resolve(index, {"A": "*", "B": "*"})` raises `ResolutionError`; it should return A 1.0.0,
   B 1.0.0, C 1.5.0 (A 2.0.0 is tried first and abandoned, and its constraint on C must be
   forgotten). Deeper dead ends are affected as well, and a real conflict must still raise.

5. Prerelease versions are selected when they should not be. `max_satisfying(["1.5.0",
   "2.0.0-beta.1"], ">=1.0.0")` returns `2.0.0-beta.1` (should be `1.5.0`), and
   `Range.filter`, `min_satisfying`, `PackageIndex.candidates` and `resolve` inherit
   it. The README rule applies: a prerelease only matches a comparator set that itself names a
   prerelease of the same major.minor.patch (`matches` already implements it).

6. Scoped package names break. `dump` writes `@org/lib@1.3.0` but `load` raises
   `LockfileError`; `parse_requirement("@org/lib@^1.2")` raises `SpecError` and
   `parse_requirement("@org/lib")` too (both should work: names split at the last `@` that is
   not the first character). Unscoped forms such as `left-pad@^1.2` and `plain` must behave
   as before.

7. `install_order` is not the lexicographically smallest valid order. For `app` -> (`x`, `b`),
   `b` -> `c` (x and c have no dependencies) it returns `["c", "x", "b", "app"]`; the README
   rule gives `["c", "b", "x", "app"]` (when `c` is done, `b` and `x` are ready and `b` is
   smaller). `install_plan` uses the same order.

Hidden checks cover each symptom, close variants through the related range forms and APIs
named above, and a broad regression suite of the current correct behaviour. Run the visible
tests with `python -m unittest discover -s tests -t .`.

The `warehouse` package (catalog, lot-based stock, reservations, pricing, shipping, orders)
has several reported bugs. Find and fix their causes; README.md documents the intended
behaviour. Keep all other existing behaviour unchanged.

Example data: `A100` Widget 10.00 (0.5 kg, taxable, tiers 10+ units 5%, 50+ units 10%) with
lots `L1` 10 units expiring day 30, `L2` 20 units expiring day 20, `L3` 5 units that never
expire (received before the others); `B200` Gadget 25.50 (2 kg) with lot `L4` of 4 units.

1. Lots that never expire are used first. `stock.lots_for("A100")` returns `L3, L2, L1`; the
   order must be `L2, L1, L3` (lots without an expiry date come after all lots that expire).
   `plan`, `place` and every FEFO decision are affected (e.g. `plan("A100", 25, now=5)` should be
   `[("L2", 20), ("L1", 5)]`, it takes from `L3`).

2. Orders can oversell when a SKU appears on more than one line. `place([("B200", 3), ("B200", 3)],
   now=1)` with only 4 units on hand succeeds and drives lot `L4` negative (or fails
   half way); it must raise `InsufficientStock` and change nothing, and `[("B200", 2), ("B200", 2)]`
   must succeed with two allocations. Multi-lot SKUs are affected too: lines
   `[("A100", 15), ("A100", 15)]` must give `L2` 15 + 5 and `L1` 10, never the same units twice.
   `Stock.plan(sku, qty, now, taken)` must honour its `taken` argument.

3. Quantity tiers start one unit too late. Buying exactly 10 widgets gets no discount: the line
   should be gross 100.00, discount 5.00, net 95.00, tax 9.50; likewise exactly 50 units earn
   the 10% tier (`tier_percent`, `price_line`, `place`).

4. Rounding is banker's rounding instead of half away from zero. `round_cents("0.025")`
   returns `0.02` (should be `0.03`) and `round_cents("0.005")` returns `0.00` (should be `0.01`).
   It shows up in discounts (0.50 at 5% -> 0.03), tax (0.25 at 10% -> 0.03), `surcharge`,
   `percent_of` and refunds.

5. Shipping brackets exclude their upper limit. A parcel of exactly 1 kg costs 9.50 (should be
   5.00), exactly 5 kg costs 18.00 (should be 9.50), exactly 20 kg costs 19.20 (should be
   18.00). An order of 10 widgets (5.0 kg) therefore pays the wrong shipping.

6. Expired reservations still block stock. After `stock.book.reserve("B200", 3, expires_at=10)`,
   `stock.available("B200", 10)` and later days still report only 1 unit available (should be
   4) until somebody calls `purge`. Placing orders, `plan` and `stock_levels` are affected;
   at `now = 9` the reservation must still hold.

7. Cancelling an order puts units back into the wrong lot. After
   `place([("A100", 25)], now=5)` (20 from `L2`, 5 from `L1`) and `cancel`, `L2` stays at 0 and
   `L1` receives all 25 units instead of the original lots getting their units back. Fix it
   for orders with several lines / SKUs as well.

Hidden checks cover each symptom, close variants through the related APIs named above, and a
broad regression suite of the current correct behaviour. Run the visible tests with
`python -m unittest discover -s tests -t .`.

Our bookkeeping library `ledgerlib` has several bugs that users reported. Please find and fix
the causes. The documented conventions are in README.md. Keep all other existing behaviour
unchanged.

1. Splitting negative amounts hands the leftover cents to the wrong parts.
   `Money(-100).allocate([1, 1, 1])` returns `[-33, -33, -34]` but should be `[-34, -33, -33]`
   (the mirror image of `Money(100).allocate([1, 1, 1])`). `Money(-100).split(3)` and any
   other negative allocation are affected; the parts still must sum to the original amount.

2. Currency conversion does not round half away from zero. With 1 EUR = 0.5 USD,
   converting `Money(25, "EUR")` gives 12 cents but should give 13, and `Money(-25, "EUR")`
   should give -13. It also happens when converting through an inverse or triangulated rate,
   and it affects everything that converts to the base currency (`Ledger.balance_in`,
   `trial_balance`, `income_statement`).

3. Rolled-up balances are too high for accounts that have postings of their own. With
   `1000` (Assets) holding 700 itself and its child `1100` holding 300, `ledger.balance("1000",
   rollup=True)` gives 1700 instead of 1000. `Chart.descendants("1000")` also seems to list
   `1000` itself, and `format_tree` / `Chart.walk()` print some accounts twice.

4. Leap years in century years are wrong. `month_range(2000, 2)` ends on 2000-02-28 instead of
   2000-02-29, `fiscal_year_range(1999, 3)` ends on 2000-02-28, and importing a CSV row dated
   `2000-02-29` fails with "bad date". (1900 and 2100 are not leap years, 2000 and 2400 are.)

5. Entries posted without tags share one tag list: after `a.add_tag("audit")` on one entry, a
   *different* entry posted without tags also reports `["audit"]`. This also happens through
   `Ledger.post`, and a list passed in by the caller must not be modified or kept
   by the entry either (mutating the caller's list later must not change the entry). A
   reversal entry must also have its own tags list, independent of the original's.

6. `parse_amount("-0.05")` returns 5 (positive) instead of -5. The same happens for any
   negative amount below one unit, e.g. `"-0.5"`, `"-$0.99"`, and for CSV rows imported with
   `import_csv`.

7. After `ledger.reverse(entry_id)` (or `reverse_many`), `ledger.balance(...)` keeps returning
   the old, cached figures until something else is posted. Reports built on balances are
   affected too (`balance_in`, `trial_balance`, `balance_sheet`, rollups, `as_of` queries).

Hidden checks cover each symptom above, close variants through the sibling APIs mentioned,
and a broad regression suite of the current correct behaviour. Run the visible tests with
`python -m unittest discover -s tests -t .`.

`logpipe` (a small log-ingestion pipeline) has several reported bugs. Find and fix their causes;
README.md documents the intended behaviour. Keep all other existing behaviour unchanged.

1. Timestamps with a UTC offset are shifted the wrong way. `parse_timestamp("2024-03-10T12:00:00+05:30")`
   returns 1710091800 but 12:00 at +05:30 is 06:30 UTC, i.e. 1710052200. Negative offsets are
   wrong too (`-08:00` must be 20:00 UTC), as are the other spellings (`+0530`, `+05`) and the
   same instants arriving through `parse_line`: logfmt / JSON `ts` values and the common-log
   `[10/Oct/2023:13:55:36 +0200]` form.

2. Percentiles are one rank too high. The 50th percentile of `[1, 2, 3, 4]` is returned as 3
   (nearest-rank says 2); the 75th as 4 (should be 3), the 95th of 1..20 as 20 (should be 19).
   `describe` and the latency statistics in `aggregate` rows inherit this.

3. Window boundaries are rounded instead of floored. `bucket_start(59.6, 60)` returns 60 and
   `bucket_start(90, 60)` returns 120; they must be 0 and 60 (the window containing the
   timestamp, aligned to the epoch; negative timestamps floor too). `tumbling` and
   `aggregate` put records into the wrong windows.

4. The deduplicator suppresses a steady stream forever. `Deduper(10)` fed one message every 4
   seconds (t = 0, 4, 8, ..., 40) lets only t=0 through; it must let through t = 0, 12, 24, 36
   (a repeat is dropped only if the key was last *emitted* less than 10 s earlier, dropped
   records do not extend the quiet period). `Pipeline` duplicate counts are affected.

5. The last partial batch is lost. `MemorySink(batch_size=2)` fed 5 records through
   `Pipeline.run` only contains 4: the final record is thrown away when the sink is closed.
   `close()` (also via `with BatchSink(...)`) must write what is still buffered, exactly once.

6. `min_level` compares level names as text. `min_level("WARN")` drops ERROR and FATAL records
   (and `min_level("INFO")` drops ERROR) because "ERROR" sorts before "WARN"
   alphabetically. Severity order is DEBUG < INFO < WARN < ERROR < FATAL.

7. Enriched records share one fields dict. After enriching two records with different fields,
   the first record shows the second one's fields too (and fields of earlier records leak into
   later ones); the `Enricher`'s `defaults` get modified as a side effect. Each record must get
   its own dict and the defaults must stay untouched.

Hidden checks cover each symptom, close variants through the related code paths named above,
and a broad regression suite of the current correct behaviour. Run the visible tests with
`python -m unittest discover -s tests -t .`.

`mdhtml` (a small markdown-to-HTML renderer) has several reported rendering bugs. Find and fix their causes; README.md documents the intended behaviour. Keep all other existing behaviour unchanged. 1. Heading ids leak between documents. `render("# Intro")` returns `

Intro

` the first time, but calling it again (or `render_document`) gives `id="intro-1"`, then `intro-2`, and so on. Each document must start fresh (duplicates inside one document still get `intro`, `intro-1`, `intro-2`), and independent `Slugger()` objects must not share state. 2. The table of contents links to the wrong heading when titles repeat. For `# Intro\n## Intro\n## Details\n# Intro`, the headings get ids `intro`, `intro-1`, `details`, `intro-2`, but `Document.toc()` links all three "Intro" entries to `#intro`. The TOC must use the headings' real ids (`outline` and the depth limits keep working). 3. Markup is applied inside code spans. `` `a*b*c` `` renders `abc` and `` `__init__` `` renders `init`; the contents of code spans must stay literal. It happens in paragraphs, headings, table cells, list items and block quotes alike, and also inside link text (`` [`a_b_c`](u) ``). Backslash escapes are affected by the same root cause: `\*not em\*` renders `not em` instead of the literal `*not em*`. 4. Attribute values are not escaped properly. `[x](http://a.com/?q="1"&b=2)` renders ``: the double quotes break the attribute (they must become `"`). Image `src` and `alt` (`![say "hi"](u.png)`) and autolinks (``) have the same problem. 5. Some loose lists render as tight. `- a\n\n- b\n- c` and `- a\n- b\n\n- c` should both render all three items wrapped in `

` (a blank line between *any* two items makes the whole list loose); today the result depends on which gap holds the blank line. Nested lists decide independently, and ordered lists are affected too. 6. Escaped pipes break tables. In `| A | B |\n|---|---|\n| a \\| b | c |` the second row should be `a | bc` (README: `\|` is a literal pipe), but the cell is cut at the pipe. It also fails in the header row (the whole table is then not recognised) and in tables written without outer pipes. 7. Fenced code blocks close too early. A four-backtick fence that contains a three-backtick line, e.g. "````\n```\ncode\n```\n````", ends at the inner "```" and leaves garbage after the block. The closing fence must use the same character and be at least as long as the opening one, in top level, block quote and list item contexts, and for `~~~~` fences too. Run the visible tests with `python -m unittest discover -s tests -t .`.

`miniql`, our small SQL-like query engine over lists of dicts, has several reported bugs. Find
and fix their causes. The intended semantics are described in README.md. Keep all other
existing behaviour unchanged.

Use this table for the examples (`db.query(sql)` returns a list of dicts):

    emp(id, name, dept, salary, bonus, city)
    1 Alice eng   100 10   Paris
    2 Bob   eng    90 NULL London
    3 Carol ops    80 5    Paris
    4 dave  ops    80 NULL Berlin
    5 Eve   sales  70 20   NULL
    6 Frank eng    90 7    London
    7 Gina  sales  70 NULL Paris

1. Mixed AND / OR is grouped wrongly. `SELECT id FROM emp WHERE dept = 'sales' OR dept = 'eng'
   AND salary > 90` returns `[1]` but should return `[1, 5, 7]` (AND binds tighter than OR).
   The same expression written in HAVING or inside a CASE condition is affected too.

2. NOT IN with a NULL in the list returns rows. `SELECT id FROM emp WHERE salary NOT IN (100,
   NULL)` should return no rows (the test is unknown for every row that does not match),
   but returns ids 2-7. `NOT (salary IN (90, NULL))` and a NULL coming from a column inside the
   list (`WHERE 5 NOT IN (bonus, 1)`) behave the same wrong way.

3. Descending order scrambles ties. `SELECT id FROM emp ORDER BY salary DESC` returns
   `[1, 6, 2, 4, 3, 7, 5]` but should return `[1, 2, 6, 3, 4, 5, 7]` (equal salaries keep
   their original relative order). With several keys the same thing happens
   (`ORDER BY dept DESC, salary DESC`, `ORDER BY dept, salary DESC`), with NULLs
   (`ORDER BY bonus DESC`) and after GROUP BY (`ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC`).

4. `LIMIT` with `OFFSET` returns too few rows. `SELECT id FROM emp ORDER BY id LIMIT 3 OFFSET
   2` returns `[3]` but should return `[3, 4, 5]`. Also check DISTINCT / GROUP BY queries.

5. LIKE treats regex characters in the pattern as special. Given a table `files(id, name)` with
   names `a.c`, `abc`, `a+b`, `aab`, `x[1]`, `x1`, `f(1)`, `f1`: `name LIKE 'a.c'` returns both
   `a.c` and `abc` (should be only `a.c`); `LIKE 'a+b'` returns `aab`; `LIKE 'x[1]'` returns
   `x1`; `LIKE 'f(1)'` fails or returns `f1`. `NOT LIKE` is affected the same way.

6. Results share row dicts with the table. `rows = db.query("SELECT * FROM emp");
   rows[0]["salary"] = 0` changes salary of employee 1 in later queries (also for
   `SELECT * ... ORDER BY/LIMIT/DISTINCT` variants). Also, after `row = {...all
   columns...}; db.insert("emp", row)`, changing `row` afterwards changes the stored data
   (same for `insert_many`).

7. ORDER BY ignores a SELECT-list alias that has the same name as a column.
   `SELECT id, salary * -1 AS salary FROM emp ORDER BY salary` should sort by the negated
   value (`[1, 2, 6, 3, 4, 5, 7]`) but sorts by the original column. `SELECT UPPER(name) AS name
   FROM emp ORDER BY name` and grouped queries such as `SELECT dept, COUNT(*) AS salary FROM
   emp GROUP BY dept ORDER BY salary, dept` are affected too. WHERE and GROUP BY must keep
   using the column.

Hidden checks cover each symptom, close variants through the related query paths named
above, and a broad regression suite of the current correct behaviour. Run the visible tests
with `python -m unittest discover -s tests -t .`.

The `throttle` package (rate limiters plus a small deterministic job scheduler, driven by a
`FakeClock`) has several reported bugs. Find and fix their causes; README.md documents the
intended behaviour. Keep all other existing behaviour unchanged.

1. A token bucket that is looked at often never refills. `b = TokenBucket(2, 0.5, clock)`
   (capacity 2, one token per 2 s): drain it with `b.try_acquire(2)`, then
   `clock.advance(1)`, `b.try_acquire()` -> False (fine), `clock.advance(1)`,
   `b.try_acquire()` -> False, but it should be True because 2 s have passed in total.
   Looking at `b.tokens` every 0.25 s with `rate=1` always shows 0.0 instead of
   0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0; `retry_after()` does not shrink as time passes; and after 1.5 s at
   `rate=1` the remaining half token is lost. The same budget loss shows up through
   `RateLimiter` for token-bucket rules.

2. A sliding-window event does not expire on time. `SlidingWindowLog(2, 10, clock)` with
   events at t=0 and t=1: at t=10 a new request should be allowed (the t=0 event is exactly
   10 s old and no longer counts) but it is denied until t=11. `count()`, `remaining()`
   and `retry_after()` are affected the same way, and so is a `RateLimiter` rule that uses
   `sliding_window`.

3. Different routes share one budget. With the policy from the README example style
   (`default`: token bucket 5/1 s, `/search`: token bucket capacity 2 rate 1, `/login`: token
   bucket capacity 1 rate 0.5), after `limiter.check("alice", "/search")` twice,
   `limiter.check("alice", "/login")` is denied and the default route is affected too; the
   `limit`, `remaining` and `retry_after` of the decisions are those of a different rule.
   Routes matched by different rules must have independent budgets (and `limiter.active()` should
   list one `(client, rule key)` entry per rule), while routes that match the same rule (e.g.
   `/api/a` and `/api/b` under `/api/*`) still share one.

4. Jobs with equal priority do not run in submission order. Scheduling `zeta`, `alpha`, `mid`
   (same priority) and calling `run_due()` runs `alpha`, `mid`, `zeta`; it should be `zeta`,
   `alpha`, `mid`. A job that failed and is retried keeps its original place in that order.

5. Back-off delays are one step too long. `Backoff(base=1, factor=2).delay(1)` is 2 but the
   first retry should wait `base` (1), then 2, 4, 8. `Backoff.schedule`, capped back-offs and the
   scheduler's retry timing (a job failing twice with `backoff=Backoff(1, 2)` should run at t=0,
   1 and 3) are affected.

6. One retry too few. `Scheduler.schedule(..., retries=3)` stops after 3 calls in total; it
   should allow 4 (the first attempt plus 3 retries), and `retry_call(fn, retries=n, ...)` has the
   same off-by-one. `retries=0` still means a single attempt.

7. `Retry-After` is rounded down. A denied decision with `retry_after == 1.5` gives header
   `"1"`, but it must be the number of whole seconds rounded up (`"2"`); `52.5` should give
   `"53"`. The minimum stays `"1"` and an impossible request still gives `"never"`.

Hidden checks cover each symptom, close variants through the related APIs named above, and a
broad regression suite of the current correct behaviour. Run the visible tests with
`python -m unittest discover -s tests -t .`.

`sheetcalc` (a small spreadsheet formula engine) has several reported bugs. Find and fix their
causes; README.md documents the intended behaviour. Keep all other existing behaviour
unchanged.

1. Column letters go wrong at multiples of 26. `index_to_col(26)` returns `"A@"` (should be
   `"Z"`), `index_to_col(52)` returns `"B@"` (should be `"AZ"`), and 702 / 18278 are wrong too.
   Everything that builds cell names from numbers is affected: `expand_range("Y1", "AB1")`
   skips or garbles `Z1`, ranges / copies / `render_grid` / `dump_csv` / `load_csv` that cross
   column Z.

2. `&` binds as tightly as `+` and `-`. `="a"&1+2` gives `#VALUE!` (should be `"a3"`),
   `=1+2&3+4` gives the number 37 instead of the text `"37"`, `="x"&2*3` gives `#VALUE!` (should
   be `"x6"`). The README lists the precedence levels.

3. Ranges whose corners are written in reverse order are empty. With A1=1, B1=2, A2=3, B2=4,
   `=SUM(B2:A1)` gives 0 instead of 10; `COUNT`, `AVERAGE`, `MAX`, `CONCAT` ... on `B2:A1` or
   `A2:B1` or `A3:A1` are affected, `expand_range("B2", "A1")` returns `[]`, and the
   formula does not recalculate when one of those cells changes.

4. `ROUND` uses banker's rounding on binary floats. `=ROUND(2.5)` gives 2 (should be 3),
   `=ROUND(-2.5)` gives -2 (should be -3), `=ROUND(0.125,2)` gives 0.12 (0.13), `=ROUND(2.675,2)` gives
   2.67 (2.68), `=ROUND(1250,-2)` gives 1200 (1300).

5. Stale values after an edit. With A1=1, B1 `=A1+1`, C1 `=B1*2`, D1 `=C1+10`: after reading D1
   (14) and setting A1 to 5, D1 still shows 14 (only B1 is refreshed; it should be 22). The
   same happens through ranges (`B1 =SUM(A1:A3)`, `C1 =B1*2`, ...), after replacing a
   middle formula by a constant, and after clearing a middle cell.

6. `IF` evaluates both branches. `=IF(TRUE,1,1/0)` gives `#DIV/0!` instead of 1;
   `=IF(A1=0,0,10/A1)` with A1=0 gives `#DIV/0!` instead of 0; `=IF(FALSE,1/0,2)`,
   `=IF(TRUE,"ok",SQRT(-4))`, nested `IF`s and `IF` used inside other functions are affected.
   An error in the *selected* branch (or in the condition) must still be the result.

7. Copying formulas mishandles mixed `$` references. With `B1` = `=A$1*2`, `copy("B1","B3")`
   should give `=A$1*2` but gives `=A$3*2`; with `B1` = `=$A1*2`, `copy("B1","B3")` should give
   `=$A3*2` but gives `=$A1*2`. Ranges (`=SUM($A1:B$2)`) and `fill_down` behave the same wrong way;
   `A1` and `$A$1` forms are fine.

Hidden checks cover each symptom, close variants through the related code paths named above,
and a broad regression suite of the current correct behaviour. Run the visible tests with
`python -m unittest discover -s tests -t .`.

`sitegen` (a static site generator working on in-memory files) has several reported bugs.
Find and fix their causes; README.md documents the intended behaviour. Keep all other existing
behaviour unchanged.

1. Front matter values that contain a colon are cut. `title: Hello: World` parses as the
   key `title: Hello` with value `World`, so the page loses its title (it must be the title
   `Hello: World`).
   Same for `subtitle: A: B: C`, URLs with ports (`url: http://x.org:8080/a`), times (`09:30`)
   and quoted values such as `q: "a: b"`.

2. Permalinks with `{month}` are not zero padded. For a post dated 2024-03-05 and the pattern
   `/blog/{year}/{month}/{day}/{slug}/` the URL is `/blog/2024/3/05/alpha/`, expected
   `/blog/2024/03/05/alpha/` (this also changes the output file paths in `Site.build()`).

3. The blog index loses posts. With 7 posts and `per_page=3`, `paginate` returns 2 pages and the
   7th post is never listed; it must return 3 pages (`ceil(n / per_page)`, at least one).
   `Site.build()` with 5 posts and `per_page: 2` writes only `blog/index.html` and
   `blog/page/2/index.html`, so the oldest post is missing.

4. Posts with the same date are listed in the wrong order. Three posts dated 2024-03-05 titled
   `Zebra`, `Alpha`, `mango` appear as Zebra, mango, Alpha on the blog index, but must appear
   as Alpha, mango, Zebra (title A to Z, case-insensitive), while newer dates still come first.
   The tag pages, feed, `by_section`, `by_year` and neighbour lookups are affected too.

5. Drafts leak into the feed and the sitemap. A page with `draft: true` is correctly missing
   from the rendered pages, the blog index and the tag pages, but its title shows up as an

Feature request for the `levelcount` CLI: add a `--min-level LEVEL` option (short form `-m`)
so noisy levels can be hidden, e.g. `python -m levelcount --min-level warning app.log`.

Required behaviour:

- Only levels at or above LEVEL are counted and shown, using the existing severity order
  DEBUG < INFO < WARNING < ERROR < CRITICAL. This applies to both the table and `--json`
  output, and the TOTAL row of the table only sums the levels that are shown.
- LEVEL is case-insensitive and accepts the same aliases as log lines (`warn`, `err`, `fatal`).
- Without the option, output is exactly as today.
- An unknown LEVEL is a usage error: argparse-style, exit status 2, and the message on stderr
  must name the bad value and list the valid levels (DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL).

`main(argv)` must keep returning the exit status for normal runs.

`svcconf.load_config()` accepts almost anything. A config with `"port": "8080"` or
`"workers": 0` loads fine and the service crashes much later, and a missing `host` surfaces as
a bare `KeyError: 'host'`. Operators need to be told exactly what is wrong, all at once.

Please add validation to `load_config()` (and therefore `load_config_file()`). Any problem
raises `svcconf.ConfigError`; its `errors` attribute lists every problem found and `str(error)`
is those messages joined with `"; "`. Messages must be exactly as below.

Schema (see README): `host` string, required, not blank; `port` integer 1..65535, required;
`workers` integer >= 1 (default 4); `log_level` one of debug, info, warning, error, matched
case-insensitively and stored lower-case (default "info"); `timeout_s` number > 0, stored as a
float (default 30.0). Booleans are never accepted as numbers.

Messages (JSON type names: string, integer, number, boolean, array, object, null; an integer
value is reported as `integer`, a non-integral number as `number`):

- text is not valid JSON (only this error is reported):
  `invalid JSON at line <L>, column <C>: <msg>` using the decoder's line, column and message
- top level is not an object (only this error is reported):
  `config must be a JSON object, got <type>`
- `unknown key '<key>'`
- `<field>: required`
- `<field>: expected <expected>, got <type>` with expected `string`, `integer` or `number`
- `host: must not be empty`
- `port: must be between 1 and 65535, got <value>`
- `workers: must be >= 1, got <value>`
- `log_level: must be one of debug, info, warning, error, got '<value>'`
- `timeout_s: must be > 0, got <value>`

`<value>` is the value as written by `json.dumps` (e.g. `70000`, `-1.5`). Order: unknown-key
errors first, sorted by key, then one error at most per field in the order host, port,
workers, log_level, timeout_s.

`tinycsv` breaks on quoted fields that contain line breaks. Exports from our ticketing system

    id,description

`parse()` raises `CSVError: line 2: unterminated quoted field` instead of returning
`[["id", "description"], ["1", "first line\nsecond line"]]`.

Please make the reader handle this properly. Required behaviour:

- A quoted field may contain the delimiter, doubled quotes (`""` -> `"`), and line breaks.
  Line breaks inside quotes are kept exactly as written (`\n` stays `\n`, `\r\n` stays `\r\n`).
- Outside quotes, a row ends at `\n` or `\r\n` only. Any other character, including a lone
  `\r` or Unicode line/paragraph separators, is ordinary field content.

  skipped, as today.
- Errors raise `CSVError` whose `line` is the 1-based physical line in the input:
  - a quoted field that is never closed -> the line where that quoted field started;
  - any character other than the delimiter or a row end directly after a closing quote
    (e.g. `"ab"c`) -> the line where that character is;
  - `parse_records()` field-count mismatch -> the line where the offending row starts

- The public API (`parse`, `parse_records`, `CSVError`) and the delimiter option stay the same.

- `missing_ids`: keeps the order of `expected` and its duplicates.
- `changed_ids`: compares each new record against the *last* record with the same id in

Ids are strings or integers. Target: each function handles 200,000 records in well under

Daily jobs drift by an hour after a daylight-saving change.

A job scheduled with `cronlite.daily_occurrences(date(2024, 3, 8), 4, time(9, 0), EASTERN)`
runs at 09:00 on March 8 and 9, but at 10:00 on March 10 and 11 (DST started on March 10).
The same happens in November in the other direction. `next_run()` is affected too because it
is built on `daily_occurrences()`.

A daily job is defined by its local wall-clock time, so every occurrence must be at `at` local
time on consecutive calendar days, with the correct UTC offset for that day. Two special cases:

- If `at` does not exist on a given day (it falls in the hour skipped when DST starts, e.g.
  02:30 on 2024-03-10 in EASTERN), the job runs at the equivalent instant after the gap,
  i.e. shifted forward by the length of the gap (02:30 becomes 03:30 EDT that day).
- If `at` happens twice on a given day (the repeated hour when DST ends, e.g. 01:30 on
  2024-11-03), the job runs once, at the first occurrence (01:30 EDT), with `fold=0`.

Returned datetimes must stay timezone-aware in the requested zone and compare/convert correctly
(e.g. `.astimezone(timezone.utc)` gives the right instant). Do not change the zone rules in
`cronlite/zones.py`, and keep the existing argument validation.

`dec.Dec` does exact decimal arithmetic only. Add arithmetic that is rounded to a precision,
implemented by you (changes touch `dec/number.py`, a new `dec/context.py` and `dec/__init__.py`).
Do NOT use or import the stdlib `decimal` (or `fractions`) module anywhere in the package.

**`Context(prec=28, rounding=ROUND_HALF_EVEN)`** (`ValueError` unless `prec` is a positive int
(not bool) and `rounding` is one of the eight constants). Export from `dec`: `Context`,
`InvalidOperation` and `DivisionByZero` (two unrelated `ArithmeticError` subclasses) and the
constants `ROUND_UP, ROUND_DOWN, ROUND_CEILING, ROUND_FLOOR, ROUND_HALF_UP, ROUND_HALF_DOWN,
ROUND_HALF_EVEN, ROUND_05UP`, whose values are exactly the strings of the same name in the
`decimal` module (`dec.ROUND_UP == "ROUND_UP"`, ...). Methods (arguments may be `Dec`, `int` or
`str`; they are converted with `Dec(x)`; results are new `Dec` objects):

`add(a, b)`, `sub(a, b)`, `mul(a, b)`, `div(a, b)` (true division), `divint(a, b)` (integer part
of the quotient, truncated toward zero), `rem(a, b)` (remainder with the sign of the dividend,
`a - b * divint(a, b)`, NOT Python's floored modulo), `quantize(a, b)` (rescale `a` to the
exponent of `b`, rounding with the context rounding) and `sqrt(a)`.

The contract is: results are IDENTICAL (sign, coefficient digits and exponent, i.e. the same
`as_tuple()` and `str`) to the corresponding methods `add, subtract, multiply, divide,
divide_int, remainder, quantize, sqrt` of `decimal.Context(prec=prec, rounding=rounding,
Emax=999999999, Emin=-999999999)` with the `InvalidOperation` and `DivisionByZero` traps enabled -
i.e. the General Decimal Arithmetic rules; exponent limits can be ignored (operands in tests have
small exponents), special values (Infinity/NaN) do not exist. The points people get wrong:
- results are computed exactly and then rounded to `prec` significant digits (a carry such as
  `9.995 -> 10.0` re-normalises); `ROUND_05UP` rounds away from zero only if the last kept digit
  would otherwise be 0 or 5; exact results are not padded.
- exponents: `add`/`sub` give the smaller exponent of the operands when the result is exact (so
  `12 + 7.00 = 19.00`), `mul` the sum; `div` gives the exact quotient with trailing zeros removed
  down to the ideal exponent `exp(a) - exp(b)` (`2.400 / 2.0 = 1.20`, `1000 / 100 = 10`) or, if
  inexact, exactly `prec` digits; `divint` has exponent 0; `rem` has exponent `min(exp(a),
  exp(b))` and is then rounded to the context precision; `quantize` gives exponent `exp(b)`
  exactly; `sqrt` of an exact square strips trailing zeros down to the ideal exponent
  `exp(a) // 2` (floor), and the correctly rounded `sqrt` ALWAYS rounds half-even whatever the
  context rounding is.
- sign of a zero result: `add`/`sub`: `-0` if both addends are negative, otherwise (for exactly
  cancelling or mixed-sign operands, including `0 + -0`) `-0` only under `ROUND_FLOOR` (two positive zeros give `0`);
  `mul`, `div`, `divint`: exclusive-or of the operand signs; `rem`: sign of the dividend;
  `quantize` and `sqrt`: sign of the operand. A zero result keeps the exponent rules above
  (`0E+3 * 0.00` is `0E+1`).
- errors: `div`/`divint` of a non-zero by zero raise `DivisionByZero`; `0/0`, `0//0` and any
  `rem` by zero raise `InvalidOperation`; so do `divint`/`rem` when the integer quotient has
  more than `prec` digits, `quantize` when the result needs more than `prec` digits (including
  after a rounding carry) and `sqrt` of a negative non-zero number.
Operators on `Dec` (`+ - *`) stay exact exactly as today, and `/` stays unsupported.

**`Dec.to_eng_string()`** (new): the General Decimal Arithmetic engineering notation
(exponent a multiple of three, same as `decimal.Decimal.to_eng_string`, including the zero cases
such as `0E+4 -> 0.00E+6`). `str(Dec)` is unchanged. Existing behaviour (parsing, `round_places`,
equality/hash, `as_tuple`, ...) must keep working. Precisions up to a few hundred digits must
work and be fast.

`textmerge` only merges at file level (`merge_text` raises `MergeConflict` as soon as both
sides changed the file) and its `diff` is a quadratic LCS table. Implement a real line-level
three-way merge (changes touch `textmerge/diff.py`, `textmerge/merge.py` and
`textmerge/__init__.py`). A *line* is a `str` that keeps its own line ending (see
`split_lines`); lines are compared including their endings.

**`diff(a, b)`**: same return format as today (list of `("=", line)`, `("-", line)`,
`("+", line)`), but it must be a *minimal* edit script (fewest `-` plus `+` operations;
among minimal scripts any is fine) and must run in roughly O((N+M)·D) time: files of 40,000
lines with a couple of hundred edits must be diffed in well under 5 seconds. `apply_diff`
keeps working.

**`merge3(base, ours, theirs, labels=("ours", "base", "theirs"), style="merge")`** takes three
lists of lines and returns a new `MergeResult` (exported) with `.lines` (list of lines),
`.conflicts` (int), `.text` (the lines joined) and `.clean` (`conflicts == 0`). Inputs are not
modified. `style` is `"merge"` or `"diff3"` (`ValueError` otherwise). Algorithm:

1. Compute the changed regions ("hunks") of `ours` and of `theirs` relative to `base` from a
   minimal diff; a hunk `(b0, b1)` says that `base[b0:b1]` (possibly empty = a pure insertion at
   `b0`) was replaced by some lines. (When the base lines are all distinct and new lines are new,
   the hunks do not depend on which minimal diff you pick; only such inputs are tested.)
2. A hunk of `ours` and a hunk of `theirs` *touch* if `b0 <= c1 and c0 <= b1` for their base
   ranges `(b0, b1)` and `(c0, c1)`, so overlapping, adjacent (`b1 == c0`) and same-point
   insertions all touch. Group hunks into clusters: the connected components of the "touches"
   relation (transitively). A cluster covers the base range from its smallest `b0` to its
   largest `b1`.
3. For each cluster compute `base_text` (the base lines of that range), `ours_text` and
   `theirs_text` (that range with the respective side's hunks applied). If `ours_text ==
   theirs_text`, or one side's text equals `base_text`, emit the other/equal text (no
   conflict). Otherwise it is a conflict. Base lines outside clusters are emitted unchanged.
4. A conflict first moves the longest common prefix of `ours_text`/`theirs_text` out of the
   markers (emitted before them), then, on the remainders, the longest common suffix (emitted
   after the markers); the markers surround what is left:
   `"<<<<<<< <labels[0]>\n"`, ours lines, [`"||||||| <labels[1]>\n"` and the *whole* `base_text`,
   only for `style="diff3"`], `"=======\n"`, theirs lines, `">>>>>>> <labels[2]>\n"`. If the
   last line of a section inside the markers lacks a trailing `"\n"`, one is appended to it
   (lines moved outside the markers are not altered). `conflicts` counts conflict blocks.

**`merge_text(base, ours, theirs, on_conflict="raise", labels=..., style="merge")`** works on
strings (split with `split_lines`) and returns the merged text. With conflicts it raises
`MergeConflict` (as today) whose new attribute `.result` is the `MergeResult`, or, with
`on_conflict="markers"`, returns the text with markers (`ValueError` for any other value).
The old behaviour for the three file-level cases (one side unchanged, or both sides equal)
is of course preserved, and `split_lines` must keep treating only `"\n"` as a line break.

`mdinline` renders a subset of inline Markdown but treats `*` and `_` as plain text. Implement emphasis and strong emphasis exactly as in the CommonMark spec 0.31.2 (section 6.2 "Emphasis and strong emphasis", rules 1-17, and the "process emphasis" delimiter-stack algorithm of the appendix). Everything the other inline constructs do today stays as is. Touch `scan.py`, `render.py`, `chars.py` and add what you need (e.g. `emphasis.py`). **Syntax in scope**: backslash escapes (`\` before an ASCII punctuation character gives that character as plain text; before anything else the backslash is literal), code spans (as implemented today; their content is never scanned for emphasis), `*`/`_` delimiter runs, and plain text. There are no links, images, raw HTML, hard line breaks or entity references (so CommonMark's bracket/link interplay does not exist here). Newlines are kept as they are and count as whitespace. **Output**: `...` and `...` exactly as CommonMark's reference HTML (one `` or `` per matched pair of 1 or 2 delimiters; `***a***` is `a`), text escaped as today (`& < > "`), code spans as `..`. Delimiters that stay unmatched are output as literal text (escaped as usual). **Details people get wrong** (all from the spec; also see the examples in the spec's section 6.2, which the hidden tests contain): - Delimiter run = maximal run of the same character (`*` or `_`) in the SOURCE text; escaped characters are not part of a run, but they ARE the neighbouring character for the flanking test, as is the backtick next to a code span. The start and the end of the text count as whitespace. - *Unicode whitespace* = category Zs or tab, line feed, form feed, carriage return. *Unicode punctuation* (spec 0.31) = ASCII punctuation or any character in the Unicode categories P or S (so `€`, `©`, `—`, `«`, `。` are punctuation, no-break space is whitespace). Use `unicodedata.category`. - left-/right-flanking and `can_open`/`can_close` for `*` and `_` as in the spec (`_` additionally needs `not right-flanking or preceded by punctuation` to open and the mirror condition to close). - Matching follows "process emphasis": for each potential closer (in order) look back for the nearest potential opener of the same character; skip an opener if the "multiple of 3" rule forbids it: if (the closer can also open OR the opener can also close) and the sum of the ORIGINAL lengths of the two delimiter runs is a multiple of 3, then they only match if both original lengths are multiples of 3. Use 2 delimiters (strong) when both sides still have at least 2, else 1 (em). Delimiters between a matched opener and closer are dropped from the stack; a closer without opener that cannot open is removed; leftover delimiters are plain text. - `plain_text(text)` (used for table-of-contents titles) must now return the text content with the emphasis markers consumed (`plain_text("*foo **bar** baz*") == "foo bar baz"`; unmatched markers stay), and `render_document` / `outline` pick the new behaviour up through `render_inline` / `plain_text`. - Large inputs: the algorithm must be linear-ish (use the spec's `openers_bottom` idea or equivalent; inputs such as `"a* " * 40000` or `"*a**" * 20000` must finish within seconds) and rendering/`plain_text` must not recurse deeper than Python allows for nesting depth: `"*" * 12000 + "x" + "*" * 12000` has to work (6,000 nested ``).

`minire` is a small backtracking regex library. It supports literals, `.`, escapes, classes
and the greedy quantifiers `* + ?` only. Extend it (parser, AST, matcher and API; you may
restructure the internals freely, only the public API below is checked) so that, for every
pattern in the grammar below, it gives the same results as Python's `re` module (same match
spans, same capture groups, same backtracking priorities). The subject strings are `str`, no
flags, no `re.MULTILINE`/`re.DOTALL`.

**Grammar** (in addition to what exists today):
- alternation `a|b|c` (lowest precedence, empty branches allowed, leftmost branch preferred);
- capturing groups `( ... )`, numbered by opening parenthesis, and non-capturing `(?: ... )`;
  any other `(?` form is a `PatternError`;
- quantifiers on any atom or group: `* + ?` and `{m}`, `{m,}`, `{,n}`, `{m,n}`, `{,}` (that is
  `*`); each can be followed by `?` to make it lazy. A `{` that does not start one of these
  forms (`a{`, `a{x}`, `{}`, `a{1,x}`) is a literal brace, as in `re`;
- anchors `^` (only at index 0 of the string, even when searching from a `pos`) and `$` (only at
  the very end of the string - not before a trailing newline); there is no multiline mode;
- backreferences `\1` ... `\9` (a backslash and one digit 1-9). A reference to a group that has
  not participated in the match fails to match. Referring to a group that is not yet closed at
  that point of the pattern (`\1(a)`, `(a\1)`, `\2` with one group) is a `PatternError`.

**Errors** (`PatternError`, a `ValueError`): unbalanced parentheses, a quantifier with nothing to
repeat (at the start of the pattern, a group or a branch, or directly after `^`/`$`, e.g. `*a`,
`(+a)`, `a|*`, `^*`, `{2}a`), a quantifier applied directly to a quantifier (`a**`, `a{2}{3}`,
`a+*`; the lazy `?` suffix is of course fine, and `a*+` need not be supported), `{m,n}` with
`m > n`, plus the errors that exist today.

**API**: `Pattern.groups` (number of capturing groups); `Match.group(n=0)` (`None` for a group that
did not participate, `IndexError` for an out-of-range or negative n), `Match.groups()` (tuple
of groups 1..n, `None` for unset), `Match.span/start/end(n=0)` (`(-1, -1)`/`-1` for unset
groups). A repeated group reports its last iteration. `Pattern.match(string, pos=0)`,
`Pattern.search(string, pos=0)`, `Pattern.fullmatch(string)` as before. New:
`Pattern.findall(string)` and `Pattern.sub(repl, string, count=0)`, plus the module-level
`minire.findall(pattern, string)` and `minire.sub(pattern, repl, string, count=0)`.
- `findall` returns the whole matches as strings if the pattern has no groups, group 1 if it
  has one, else a tuple of all groups; a group that did not participate gives `''`.
- Scanning (for both `findall` and `sub`) follows Python 3.7+ rules: matches are non-overlapping
  and found left to right. After a non-empty match ending at `e` the next search starts at `e`
  and may find an empty match there. After an EMPTY match at `e` the next search starts at `e`
  too, but a match that is empty at `e` is rejected (the matcher backtracks into other
  alternatives and may return a non-empty match starting at `e`); if none exists the scan moves
  on to `e + 1`. E.g. `findall(r"^|\w+", "foo")` is `['', 'foo']`.
- `sub(repl, string, count=0)`: `repl` is a string inserted literally (no backslash processing)
  or a callable taking the `Match`; `count=0` means all matches, otherwise at most `count`.

**Empty loops**: a quantified body that can match the empty string (`(a*)*`, `(a|)+`) must
terminate; for such patterns only the overall match span is compared with `re`, not the group
contents.

**Scale**: the matcher must not rely on Python recursion depth proportional to the subject length.
Subjects of 60,000 characters must work for patterns such as `.*x`, `(?:a|b)*c`, `(a|b)*c`,
`x*?y`, `(ab)*b?`, `^((?:xy)*)\|\1$` and `\w+` with `findall` (each within a few seconds).
Counted repeats up to a few hundred (`a{50,200}`, `(?:ab){100}`) must work.

`layout.format_paragraph` fills lines greedily, which gives ragged paragraphs. Add an optimal
line breaker and the options around it (changes touch `layout/paragraph.py`, `layout/align.py`,
a new module for the breaker, and `layout/__init__.py`). All widths are `len()` of the text.

New signature: `format_paragraph(text, width, align="left", indent=0, first_indent=None,
method="greedy")` returning a list of lines (and `format_text(text, width, **kwargs)` passing the
same options through to every paragraph). `indent` spaces start every line except the first,
which starts with `first_indent` spaces (default: `indent`); both must satisfy `0 <= x < width`
and `width >= 1`, `method` must be `"greedy"` or `"optimal"`, `align` one of `left`, `right`,
`center`, `justify`; anything else is a `ValueError` (for text that has at least one line). The available width of the first line is `width -
first_indent`, of the other lines `width - indent`. Text is split into words with `str.split()`.
`method="greedy"` keeps today's behaviour (a word fills the current line if it fits, never
breaks inside a word), except that it now honours `first_indent` too. Existing functions
(`wrap`, `justify_words`, `align_line`, ...) keep working.

**`method="optimal"`** breaks the paragraph so that the total badness is minimal.
- *Boxes*: every word is cut after each `-` that has an ASCII-alphanumeric character on both
  sides (`state-of-the-art` -> `state-`, `of-`, `the-`, `art`; `a--b`, `-x`, `x-` are not cut). The
  hyphen stays at the end of its piece. Consecutive boxes of one word are joined without a
  space; boxes of different words are separated by one space. A line is a run of consecutive
  boxes; its natural length is the sum of the box lengths plus one per space between them.
  A line may end after any box.
- *Feasible lines*: natural length <= the available width of that line, or a line consisting
  of one single box (which may then be too wide).
- *Cost*: the last line costs 0. Any other line costs `(available - natural) ** 2`, except a
  single over-wide box which costs 0. Minimise the sum of the costs over all layouts made of
  feasible lines. Among layouts with the same minimal cost choose the one whose sequence of line
  lengths (counted in boxes) is lexicographically LARGEST (longest first line first, then
  longest second line, ...).
- It must handle a paragraph of 40,000 words (width 72) in a few seconds: a line only has to
  consider as many boxes as can fit.

**Alignment** (both methods; the line text excludes the indentation, `avail` is that line's
available width, and no line ever has trailing spaces):
- `left`: the natural text. `right`: `avail - len` spaces (none if negative) before the text.
  `center`: `(avail - len) // 2` spaces before the text (none if negative).
- `justify`: every line except the last is stretched to exactly `avail` columns (if it is
  not already that wide): the extra spaces `e = avail - natural` are shared over the *space*
  gaps between words (joins after a hyphen inside a word are not gaps): each gap gets `e //
  gaps` extra and the first `e % gaps` gaps (from the left) one more. A line without a space gap
  (one box, or one hyphenated word) is left as is; the last line is left-aligned.
  This is the rule the existing `justify_words` already uses.

`crdtext`'s `Session` applies edits in arrival order, which corrupts concurrent edits. Add a
replicated text type that converges without a server: an RGA (Replicated Growable Array)
sequence CRDT (new modules `crdtext/ops.py`, `crdtext/replica.py`, export `Op` and `Replica`
from the package; `Document` and `Session` stay unchanged).

**`Op`** - an immutable (frozen dataclass-like, hashable, `==` by value) record
`Op(kind, id=None, ref=None, char=None)`:
- insert: `Op("ins", id=(counter, replica_id), ref=<id of the element it goes after, or None for
  the start of the text>, char=<one character>)`;
- delete: `Op("del", id=None, ref=<id of the element to delete>, char=None)`.
`op.to_dict()` gives a JSON-friendly dict (`{"kind", "id": [counter, replica], "ref": [...]|None,
"char"}` for inserts, `{"kind": "del", "ref": [...]}` for deletes) and `Op.from_dict(d)`
restores an equal `Op` (lists become tuples again, also after a JSON round trip).

**`Replica(replica_id)`** (`replica_id` a non-empty `str`, else `ValueError`):
- `text()`, `len(replica)`, `visible_ids()` (ids of the visible characters in order),
  `pending()` (number of buffered operations), `history()` (list of the operations applied so far
  in the order they were applied, local ones included; a copy).
- Ids are compared as plain tuples `(counter, replica_id)`.
- `insert(index, char)` -> `Op`: `char` must be a one-character `str` (`ValueError`), `0 <=
  index <= len` (`IndexError`). The new element goes in front of the visible character that is
  currently at `index`, i.e. its `ref` is the id of the visible character at `index - 1` (None for
  index 0; deleted characters are not counted). Its counter is `1 + c`, where `c` is the largest
  counter of all insert operations this replica has APPLIED so far (0 if none; buffered operations do
  not count). The operation is applied locally and returned.
- `insert_text(index, s)` -> list of the ops of inserting the characters of `s` one after the other
  at `index, index + 1, ...` (`[]` for an empty string). `delete(index)` -> `Op("del", ref=<id of the
  visible character at index>)`, `IndexError` unless `0 <= index < len`; applied and returned.
- `apply(op)` applies an operation received from anywhere (any order, any number of times) and
  returns how many operations were newly applied by this call (an unblocked buffered operation
  counts; `0` for duplicates and for operations that had to be buffered; `ValueError` for an
  unknown kind). An insert needs its `ref` element (if any) to exist, a delete needs its target to
  exist; otherwise it is buffered (once, however often it is delivered) until the element arrives and
  is then applied automatically. An insert with an already known id and a delete of an already
  deleted element are duplicates. Deletion only hides the element (tombstone); a later insert may
  still use a deleted element as its `ref`.
- Ordering rule (this is what makes all replicas converge): the elements form a tree in which each
  insert is a child of its `ref` element (None = root). The text is the pre-order depth-first walk of
  that tree in which the children of a node are visited in DESCENDING id order (the newest sibling
  first), skipping deleted elements. Consequently the final text depends only on the SET of
  operations, never on their arrival order, and concurrent runs of typing at the same place do not
  interleave (e.g. A types `abc` and B types `xyz` at index 0 concurrently: `xyzabc` since
  `(1, "B") > (1, "A")`). An efficient incremental way to get this order is the classic RGA
  integration: put the new element right after its `ref`, skipping over every following element whose
  id is greater than the new id.
- Performance: 15,000 random local inserts/deletes, then applying all those operations in random
  order (many get buffered) or in reverse order on another replica, must each take only a few
  seconds, as must 20,000 sequential inserts at one place (so no O(n) work per operation in
  Python code is affordable for the index lookups).

`editbuf` (changes touch `editbuf/buffer.py`, `editbuf/history.py` and `editbuf/__init__.py`)
keeps all text in one Python `str`, so edits and line queries are O(file size), and it has no
markers, no `replace` and no undo groups. Extend it as follows without changing the existing
behaviour (offsets are character offsets, lines are separated by `"\n"` only).

**`Buffer`**
- `replace(start, end, s)`: exactly `delete(start, end)` followed by `insert(start, s)`, but
  validated up front. Every mutator and query validates its arguments before changing anything
  and raises `ValueError` for out-of-range or reversed positions/ranges/lines/columns (as
  today). Inserting or deleting nothing is a valid no-op.
- Markers: `add_marker(pos, gravity="left")` returns a `Marker` (exported) with attributes
  `pos`, `gravity` (`"left"` or `"right"`, `ValueError` otherwise; `pos` must be a valid offset)
  and `alive`. A marker follows edits: on `insert(p, s)` a marker with `pos > p` moves by
  `len(s)`, one with `pos == p` moves only if its gravity is `"right"`, others stay; on
  `delete(a, b)` a marker with `pos >= b` moves left by `b - a`, one with `a < pos < b` moves to
  `a`, others stay. `replace` applies those two rules in sequence (so a marker inside the
  replaced range ends at `start` for gravity `"left"` and after the new text for `"right"`).
  `remove_marker(marker)` stops tracking it (`alive` becomes `False`, `pos` keeps its last
  value; removing twice is fine).
- Scale: a buffer of about 4 million characters (150,000 lines) must take 20,000 random inserts and
  deletes (with a few markers registered) in a few seconds, `offset_to_line_col`,
  `line_col_to_offset`, `line_range` and `line_text` must be fast on it (thousands of queries
  in a few seconds), and building a buffer from a 6,000,000-character string and reading it back
  must not be slow. Appending/inserting into a 3,000,000-character single line 6,000 times must
  also be fast. (A rope, piece table, gap buffer or chunk list with per-chunk newline counts
  are all fine; correctness at chunk boundaries is tested.)

**`History`** (undo/redo of the edits made *through it*; edits applied directly to the buffer
behind its back are not supported)
- new `replace(start, end, s)`; `insert`/`delete`/`replace` that change nothing (empty text and
  empty range) record nothing; invalid arguments raise `ValueError` and record nothing.
- Groups: `begin_group()` / `end_group()` and the context manager `with history.group():`.
  Edits inside a group (nesting flattens into the outermost group) form ONE undo step, undone in
  reverse order and redone in original order. An empty group records nothing (and does not
  clear the redo stack). `end_group()` without a matching `begin_group()`, and `undo()`/`redo()`
  while a group is open, raise `RuntimeError`. The context manager closes the group even if the
  body raises.
- Recording an edit clears the redo stack (as today). Undo applies the inverse of each recorded
  edit through `Buffer.replace` and redo re-applies each edit through `Buffer.replace`, so markers
  follow undo/redo exactly like they follow normal edits (e.g. undoing a deletion re-inserts the
  text at the deletion point: a `"left"` marker there stays before it, a `"right"` marker ends up after
  it; they are not restored to their old positions). `undo()`/`redo()` return whether
  something was done; `can_undo` / `can_redo` as today.

`minisql` only runs `SELECT cols FROM t WHERE col op literal [AND ...] [ORDER BY col] [LIMIT n]`.
Turn it into a real (small) SQL SELECT engine. The hidden tests compare thousands of generated
queries with SQLite 3 (Python's `sqlite3`), so wherever this text is silent the answer is
"what SQLite does". You may restructure `lexer.py`, `parser.py`, `engine.py` freely; keep the
public API (`Database.create_table/insert/execute`, `Result.columns/.rows`, `SqlError`) and the
old queries working (`WHERE col = NULL` etc. now simply follow SQL three-valued logic, which
gives the same answers as before). Values are `int`, `float`, `str` and `None` (NULL); tables
hold one type per column (plus NULLs), so mixed-type comparisons and implicit text<->number
conversions are not tested. Identifiers and keywords are case-insensitive; string literals use
`'...'` with `''` as an escaped quote; an optional trailing `;`.

**Grammar**
`SELECT [DISTINCT|ALL] item, ... [FROM source] [WHERE e] [GROUP BY e, ...] [HAVING e]
[ORDER BY e [ASC|DESC], ...] [LIMIT e [OFFSET e]]`
- item: `*`, `alias.*`, or `expr [[AS] name]`. FROM is optional (`SELECT 1 + 1` is one row).
- source: `table [[AS] alias]` followed by any number of `, table`, `[INNER] JOIN t ON e`,
  `LEFT [OUTER] JOIN t ON e`, `CROSS JOIN t` (no ON; `JOIN` without `ON` is allowed for
  inner/cross, `LEFT JOIN` requires `ON`). Tables may be repeated under different aliases.
  Unqualified column names must be unambiguous (`SqlError` otherwise); `alias.col` and
  `table.col` (when the table has no alias) work.
- expressions (highest to lowest precedence; all binary operators are left-associative):
  unary `-` `+`; `||`; `* / %`; `+ -`; `< <= > >=`; `= != <> IS [NOT] expr, [NOT] IN (list),
  [NOT] LIKE, [NOT] BETWEEN a AND b, IS [NOT] NULL`; `NOT`; `AND`; `OR`. Note that `||` binds
  tighter than `*` as in SQLite (`2 * 3 || 4` is 68), comparisons are left-associative (`1 < 2 = 1`),
  and `NOT a = b` is `NOT (a = b)`. The operands of BETWEEN/LIKE/IN bind at the `< <= > >=`
  level or tighter.
  Literals: integers, decimals like `1.5`, strings, `NULL`. Functions: `coalesce(a, b, ...)` (2+
  args), `ifnull`, `nullif`, `abs`, `length`, `upper`, `lower` (ASCII), `substr(s, start[, len])`
  (SQLite semantics; tests use start >= 1 and len >= 0), `CASE WHEN c THEN v ... [ELSE e] END`
  and `CASE x WHEN v THEN ... END`. Aggregates `count(*)`, `count(e)`, `count(DISTINCT e)`,
  `sum`, `avg`, `min`, `max` (also with DISTINCT where it makes sense; one argument only).
  Unknown functions, wrong argument counts, unknown tables/columns, syntax errors, aggregates in
  WHERE, trailing garbage, several statements: `SqlError`.

**Semantics (SQLite)**: NULL propagates through arithmetic, comparison, `||`, functions; AND/OR/NOT
use three-valued logic; WHERE/HAVING/ON/CASE keep a row only when the condition is true (non-zero
number). Comparison results, AND/OR/NOT/IN/LIKE/BETWEEN/IS yield integers 1/0 (or NULL). `x IN
(list)`: empty list is 0, a match is 1, otherwise NULL if x or any list item is NULL, else 0;
`NOT IN` negates (NULL stays NULL). `BETWEEN` is `x >= lo AND x <= hi`. Integer `/` truncates
toward zero, `%` takes the sign of the dividend, division or modulo by zero gives NULL;
int op float is float. `LIKE` is case-insensitive for ASCII with `%` and `_`, no escape
character. Ordering and MIN/MAX use NULL < numbers < text; ORDER BY puts NULLs first for ASC and
last for DESC; ties may come in any order (tests make orderings total). ORDER BY terms may be an
integer ordinal of the select list, a select alias, or any expression. LIMIT/OFFSET take constant
integer expressions; a negative LIMIT means no limit, a negative OFFSET is 0.
`SUM` of no non-NULL values is NULL, of ints an int, otherwise float; `AVG` is a float or NULL;
`COUNT` never NULL; an aggregate query without GROUP BY always returns exactly one row (even over
no input), with GROUP BY one row per distinct key (NULLs form one group; HAVING filters groups; a
HAVING without GROUP BY is allowed). Non-aggregated, non-grouped columns in an aggregate query are
not tested. LEFT JOIN null-extends unmatched left rows (ON decides matching, WHERE filters
afterwards). DISTINCT removes duplicate output rows.

**Result columns**: `Result.columns` lists, per select item, its alias; else the column name
(lower-case, as stored) for a plain column reference; else the exact source text of the
expression from its first to its last token (`select a + 1 ...` gives `"a + 1"`). `*`
expands to the column names of every source in FROM order, `alias.*` to one source's columns.

Performance: GROUP BY over 20,000 rows and a 20,000 x 50 join must finish within seconds
(do not re-scan the whole right table through Python-level expression re-parsing for each row).

`cfgkit` loads INI and JSON configuration; add TOML support. The project supports Python 3.8+,
so you must write the parser yourself: do not import (or shell out to) `tomllib`, `tomli`,
`toml`, `tomlkit` or any other TOML library, in any module of the package.

**`cfgkit/toml.py`** (new): `loads(text) -> dict` implements TOML v1.0.0 and must behave exactly
like a conforming parser (for example Python 3.11's `tomllib`, which is what the hidden tests
compare against) on every valid and invalid document, with ONE deliberate exception: date,
time and date-time values are not supported and raise `ParseError`. In detail:
- comments, bare/quoted/dotted keys (whitespace allowed around the dots), basic, literal,
  multi-line basic and multi-line literal strings with all escape rules (`\b \t \n \f \r \" \\
  \uXXXX \UXXXXXXXX`, line-ending backslash trimming, the first newline after the opening
  delimiter trimmed, up to two quotes next to the closing delimiter, unicode escapes must be
  scalar values), integers (decimal with underscores, no leading zeros, `0x`/`0o`/`0b`),
  floats (fraction/exponent/underscores, `inf`, `nan` with optional sign), booleans, arrays
  (any mix of types, newlines, comments and a trailing comma allowed), inline tables (one line,
  no trailing comma), `[table]` and `[[array of tables]]` headers;
- control characters (other than tab, and newline where allowed) in strings and comments are errors;
  a `\r\n` line ending is treated exactly like `\n` everywhere (also inside multi-line strings);
  a lone `\r` is an error;
- every TOML rule about what may be defined where: duplicate keys; redefining a table; tables
  created implicitly by `[a.b.c]` or by dotted keys; dotted-key tables cannot be reopened with a
  `[header]` but sub-tables of them can be added; inline tables and static arrays are immutable
  (no extending them by dotted keys, `[a.b]` headers or `[[a]]`); an `[[array of tables]]` header
  starts a new element and forgets the table flags of the previous element; a header cannot
  turn a value into a table, and so on.
Return plain `dict`/`list`/`str`/`int`/`float`/`bool` objects (an integer never becomes a float).

**Errors**: any problem raises `cfgkit.ParseError` (the existing class) whose `.line` is the
1-based line on which the statement containing the problem STARTS (the line of the key or the
`[` of the header, counted after treating `\r\n` as a newline), also for errors inside a
multi-line string, array or on a later line of the same statement. Parsing a non-`str` raises
`ParseError`. The parser must be linear-time enough to read a document of 60,000 lines (and
keep a line counter that is not quadratic) within a few seconds.

**Integration**: `load_text(text, "toml")` and `load_file` for the suffix `.toml` (case-insensitive,
UTF-8, like the existing formats, so `load_layers` can mix ini/json/toml files);
`Config.from_toml(text)`; `cfgkit.loads_toml` exported from the package;
`Config.get(path, default)` now also walks lists: a path component made only of decimal digits
indexes a list (`"servers.1.host"`), an out-of-range index or a non-numeric component on a list
counts as missing (default / `KeyError`) and `Config.__contains__` follows the same rule.
Existing INI/JSON/Config behaviour is unchanged.

`urikit` splits URIs and has a simplified `join`. Make it a proper RFC 3986 implementation
(changes touch `urikit/uri.py`, `urikit/join.py`/a new resolver module, `urikit/linkset.py` and
`urikit/__init__.py`). Everything below refers to RFC 3986; use its definitions literally.

**`parse(text)`** now validates and raises `UriError` (a `ValueError`) for text that is not a
valid URI-reference. The split is still RFC appendix B, `Uri` stays a namedtuple of
`(scheme, authority, path, query, fragment)` with `None` for absent parts and `""` for present
but empty ones, and `str(uri)` recomposes per section 5.3 (so `str(parse(s)) == s` for every
valid `s`). Validity: a non-string is a `UriError`; the scheme (text before the first `:` when
that comes before any `/ ? #`) must match `ALPHA *( ALPHA / DIGIT / "+" / "-" / "." )`; without a
scheme and authority the first path segment must not contain `:`; userinfo is
`*( unreserved / pct-encoded / sub-delims / ":" )`; the host is a reg-name
(`unreserved / pct-encoded / sub-delims`) or an IP-literal in brackets whose content is either
IPv6-ish (only hex digits, `:` and `.`, with at least two `:`) or IPvFuture (`v` HEXDIG+ `.` then
one or more of unreserved / sub-delims / `:`); the port is digits only (possibly empty); path
characters are `pchar` and `/`; query and fragment are `pchar`, `/` and `?`. Every `%` must be
followed by two hex digits. Anything else (spaces, the characters `< > " { } | ^`, backslash and backtick, non-ASCII
characters, `[` / `]` outside an IP literal, `@` in the host, ...) is a `UriError`. `Uri` gains properties `userinfo`,
`host` (as written, brackets included for IP literals; `""` for an empty host), `port` (an `int`;
`None` if absent or empty) - all `None` when there is no authority - and keeps `is_absolute`.

**`remove_dot_segments(path)`**: exactly the input-buffer/output-buffer algorithm of section
5.2.4 (including its behaviour on rootless paths: `a/../../b` becomes `/b`).

**`resolve(base, ref)`** (strings): the strict algorithm of section 5.2.2 with merge (5.2.3) and
recomposition (5.3). Both are validated (`UriError`); `base` must have a scheme (fragment
ignored). Scheme and host case, percent-encoding and so on are NOT touched by `resolve`.
`join(base, ref)` stays and is now identical to `resolve`. All examples of RFC section 5.4 hold
(including `http:g` staying `http:g` in strict mode).

**`normalize(text)`** (input must be an absolute URI, else `UriError`) applies, in this order:
(1) lowercase the scheme; (2) in every component, uppercase the hex digits of each percent
encoding and decode those that encode an unreserved character (`ALPHA DIGIT - . _ ~`), then
lowercase the host (userinfo, path, query, fragment keep their case); (3) `remove_dot_segments`
on the path; (4) scheme-based rules: drop the port when it is empty (`:` alone) or its integer value is
the scheme's default (`http` 80, `https` 443, `ftp` 21, `ws` 80, `wss` 443; other ports are kept
exactly as written, e.g. `:00081`), and for those five schemes an empty path becomes `/` when
an authority is present. An empty query `?` / empty fragment `#` are kept. Percent-decoding
happens before dot-segment removal (`/%2e%2e/` is a dot segment). `equivalent(a, b)` is
`normalize(a) == normalize(b)`. Inputs where dot-segment removal would turn an authority-less
path into one starting with `//` are not tested.

**`collect_links(base, hrefs)`** (used by the crawler) changes to: `base` must be a valid absolute
URI (`UriError` otherwise); each href is stripped of leading/trailing ASCII whitespace
(space, tab, newline, carriage return, form feed), resolved against `base`, has its fragment
removed, and is normalised; hrefs that are invalid are silently skipped, as are links whose
scheme (after normalisation) is not `http` or `https`; duplicates (after normalisation) are
dropped keeping the first occurrence. Export `resolve`, `normalize`, `equivalent` and
`remove_dot_segments` from the package.

`keepcache.LRUCache` misbehaves in production, where it is shared by many worker threads:

- It is not least-recently-*used*: `get()` does not mark an entry as recently used, so hot
  entries get evicted.
- Re-`put()`-ting an existing key evicts an unrelated entry even though the cache did not grow,
  and afterwards the cache occasionally crashes with `KeyError` during eviction.
- Under concurrent use, statistics drift, `len()` can exceed the capacity, and
  `get_or_compute()` runs the expensive `compute` function many times for the same key when
  several threads miss on it at once.

Please make `LRUCache` correct and thread-safe, keeping its public API. Required behaviour:

1. `get()` and `get_or_compute()` hits mark the entry most recently used; `peek()` and
   `in` / `len()` never change recency or statistics.
2. `put()` of an existing key replaces the value, marks it most recently used and never evicts.
   A new key evicts exactly the least recently used entry when the cache is full.
3. `on_evict(key, value)` is called once per capacity eviction (not for replacements or
   `clear()`), with the evicted pair, in eviction order. The callback may call methods of the
   same cache without deadlocking.
4. `stats()`: every `get()` counts as exactly one hit or one miss; `evictions` counts capacity
   evictions. Counters stay exact under concurrency.
5. `get_or_compute(key, compute)`: when many threads miss on the same key concurrently,
   `compute(key)` runs only once and every caller gets its result. If `compute` raises, the
   exception propagates, nothing is cached, and a later call tries again. Computing one key
   must not block callers that are working with other, already cached keys.
6. All methods are safe to call from any number of threads; the cache never holds more than
   `capacity` entries.

Invoice totals are off by a cent. `ledgerfmt` does its arithmetic with binary floats:

- `format_money(2.675)` gives `$2.67`, and `format_money("0.125")` gives `$0.12`; the
  documented rule is that halves round away from zero, so these must be `$2.68` and `$0.13`.
- `total(["0.10", "0.20"])` is `0.30000000000000004`.
- `split("100.00", 3)` returns three shares of 33.33 that add up to 99.99.
- `format_money(-0.001)` prints `-$0.00`.

Please switch the module to `decimal.Decimal`. Required behaviour:

- All functions accept `int`, `str`, `Decimal` and `float`. A float is interpreted by its
  shortest repr (`2.675` means `Decimal("2.675")`, not the binary expansion).
- `format_money` rounds half away from zero to the currency's minor unit, keeps the existing
  output format (symbol, thousands separators, leading `-` for negatives), and never prints a
  negative zero: anything that rounds to zero is formatted without a sign.
- `total()` returns the exact sum as a `Decimal` (no rounding).
- `split(amount, parts, currency)` returns a list of `Decimal` shares quantised to the
  currency's minor unit that add up exactly to `amount` rounded (half away from zero) to that
  unit. Shares differ by at most one minor unit; the larger shares come first. Negative
  amounts are split the same way with the signs flipped.
- Unsupported currencies and `parts < 1` still raise `ValueError`.

Pagination in `pagekit.paginate()` is broken in two ways:

1. Every page comes back one item short. With 10 items and `per_page=3`, page 1 should contain
   items 1-3, but it only contains items 1-2.
2. The last, partially filled page is unreachable. With 10 items and `per_page=3` there should be
   4 pages (the last one holding a single item), but `total_pages` is 3 and asking for page 4
   raises `PageOutOfRange`.

Expected behaviour (pages are 1-based):

- `total_pages` is the number of pages needed to show every item, and is at least 1: an empty
  sequence has exactly one (empty) page, so `paginate([], 1)` returns a page with no items.
- `has_prev` / `has_next` tell whether a previous / next page exists.
- Requesting a page below 1 or above `total_pages` raises `PageOutOfRange`.
- `per_page` below 1 still raises `ValueError`.

Please fix `paginate()` without changing its signature or the `Page` fields.

`archpath.normalize()` gives different answers depending on the OS it runs on, which breaks
archives that are created on one platform and extracted on another:

- On Windows, `normalize("docs/a.txt")` returns `docs\a.txt`, so members no longer match the
  manifest, which uses forward slashes.
- On Linux and macOS, `normalize("docs\..\..\secret")` is accepted unchanged, although an
  archive written on Windows means "go two levels up" here, and `C:\temp\x` is accepted as a
  relative name.
- On every OS, a legitimate file named `..config` is rejected as escaping the root.

Please make `normalize()`, `split_parts()` and `is_safe()` behave identically on every OS,
without touching the filesystem. Rules:

- Both `/` and `\` are separators.
- Empty components and `.` are dropped; `..` removes the previous component. A `..` that would
  go above the root raises `UnsafePathError`, even if later components would come back down
  (`a/../../a/b` is unsafe).
- Absolute paths raise `UnsafePathError`: anything starting with a separator (including UNC
  forms like `\\server\share` and `//server/share`) and anything whose first component starts
  with a drive letter and a colon (`C:`, `c:\x`, `C:foo`, `d:/x`).
- A NUL character anywhere raises `UnsafePathError`.
- The result joins the remaining components with `/`: no leading or trailing separator, and
  `""` for paths that resolve to the root (`""`, `.`, `a/..`, `./`). Component text, including
  case, spaces and names such as `..config`, `a..b` or `...`, is kept exactly.
- `split_parts()` returns the components of the normalised path (`[]` for the root);
  `is_safe()` returns False exactly when `normalize()` would raise.

`verso` only understands plain `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`. Our registry now publishes pre-releases
and build metadata (`2.0.0-rc.1`, `1.4.0+build.7`), and `parse()` rejects them, so the release
tooling crashes.

Please implement full Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 support (sections 2, 9, 10 and 11 of the
spec) in `verso/version.py`, keeping the public API (`Version`, `parse`, `compare`,
`sort_versions`):

- `parse()` accepts `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH[-PRERELEASE][+BUILD]` and fills `Version.prerelease`
  and `Version.build` with the dot-separated identifiers as strings. It raises `ValueError` for
  anything that is not a valid semver string, including: empty identifiers (`1.0.0-alpha..1`,
  `1.0.0-`, `1.0.0+`), characters outside `[0-9A-Za-z-]` in identifiers, leading zeros in the
  numeric core (`01.2.3`) or in numeric pre-release identifiers (`1.0.0-alpha.01`), a `v`
  prefix, and surrounding whitespace. Build identifiers may have leading zeros (`1.0.0+001`).
- Precedence follows the spec exactly: a pre-release version has lower precedence than the
  associated normal version; pre-release identifiers are compared left to right, numeric
  identifiers numerically (no size limit), alphanumeric ones lexically in ASCII order, numeric
  identifiers always lower than alphanumeric ones, and a larger set of identifiers wins when
  all preceding ones are equal. Build metadata is ignored for precedence.
- `compare()` returns -1, 0 or 1 and accepts `Version` objects or strings. `==`, `<`, `>` etc.
  on `Version` follow precedence (so `1.0.0+a == 1.0.0+b`), and `hash()` is consistent with `==`.
- `str(parse(s)) == s` for every valid `s`.
- `sort_versions()` sorts by precedence and keeps the input order for versions of equal
  precedence.
